common_misconceptions.topic: Shifts versus movements along demand/supply curves
common_misconceptions.misconception: The single most common and most heavily penalised error. A change in the good's OWN PRICE causes a MOVEMENT ALONG the curve (an extension or contraction). A change in any OTHER factor (income, tastes, price of other goods, costs of production, technology, taxes) SHIFTS the whole curve. Students who 'shift demand because price rose' lose diagram and analysis marks throughout both papers.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Economics specification (8136), sections 3.1.3.1 and 3.1.3.2.

common_misconceptions.topic: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative, not all alternatives
common_misconceptions.misconception: Opportunity cost is the value of the NEXT best alternative forgone — singular, the one thing you would otherwise have chosen — not the sum of everything given up. Students routinely define it as 'what you give up', which loses the precision mark.

common_misconceptions.topic: Price elasticity of demand — the formula and the sign
common_misconceptions.misconception: PED = percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. Students invert the formula (price over quantity) or forget that the answer is normally negative (because of the inverse relationship) and that we judge elastic/inelastic by the size of the number ignoring the sign: greater than 1 is elastic, between 0 and 1 is inelastic. Quantitative skills are 15% of marks, so the calculation must be exact.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Economics specification (8136), section 3.1.3.5 and section 6 Quantitative skills.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Production is the TOTAL amount produced; productivity is output PER unit of input (usually output per worker). A firm can raise production by hiring more workers without raising productivity. Conflating the two loses analysis marks on cost and competitiveness questions.

Nominal GDP is measured at current prices and rises with inflation even if no more is produced; real GDP strips out inflation and is the true measure of growth. Students treat any rise in GDP as growth without checking it is REAL. GDP per capita (per head) matters for living standards.

Demand-pull inflation is caused by total demand rising faster than supply ('too much money chasing too few goods'); cost-push inflation is caused by rising costs of production (wages, raw materials, a weaker pound) pushing prices up. Students must identify the CAUSE correctly to recommend the right policy, since the appropriate response differs.

Fiscal policy is the GOVERNMENT changing TAXATION and SPENDING. Monetary policy is the BANK OF ENGLAND (the Monetary Policy Committee) changing INTEREST RATES and the money supply. Students mix the two up — attributing interest-rate decisions to 'the government' or tax changes to 'the Bank of England' — and lose application marks.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Economics specification (8136), sections 3.2.3.1 and 3.2.3.2.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A Strong Pound makes Imports Cheap and Exports Dear (SPICED); a weak pound does the reverse (WPIDEC). Students reason backwards. They must trace the effect through to importers, exporters and consumers, not just state the direction.

common_misconceptions.topic: Social cost is private cost PLUS external cost
common_misconceptions.misconception: Social cost = private cost + external cost. A negative externality exists when social cost exceeds private cost — the market under-prices the harm and over-produces. Students who treat 'externality' as just 'pollution' without the private/external/social framework cannot analyse intervention correctly.

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice: Each paper opens with multiple-choice questions. Candidates leave items blank rather than committing — there is no negative marking, so always select the best answer. Watch for 'which of the following is NOT' phrasing.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Define / State: A definition question wants the precise economic meaning, not an everyday paraphrase. Use the technical term in the definition (e.g. opportunity cost = 'the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made').
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Calculate: Quantitative skills are 15% of the qualification. Show the formula, substitute the figures, and give the answer with the correct unit or sign (a percentage, an index number, a PED value). One mark is often for method, one for the correct answer — never leave a calculation blank.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Explain: Make a point and develop it with a logical chain — 'this leads to... which means... therefore...'. A single undeveloped statement caps at one mark.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain: Usually data- or context-applied. Two developed points, or one point developed twice, each linked back to the named firm, market or scenario in the source material. Use the data.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Analyse (Extended Response): Analyse means build a logical chain of cause and effect, ideally with a diagram where relevant (demand/supply, PPD). Candidates list points without connecting them. Two well-developed chains beat six unconnected assertions.
student_errors_by_question_type.9 marks — Evaluate (Extended Response): Evaluate requires analysis of BOTH sides and a SUPPORTED judgement. Candidates describe advantages and stop. Weigh the arguments, consider 'it depends on...' factors (the size of the change, the time period, elasticity, the state of the economy), and reach a justified conclusion.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Evaluate (Extended Response): The highest-tariff question. Top answers sustain two or more developed arguments on each side, apply economic terminology and a diagram accurately, and reach a judgement that genuinely weighs the strongest points rather than restating them. The judgement must be present and justified, not implied.

topic_weighting_notes: The qualification is two equally-weighted written papers, each 50% of the GCSE. Paper 1 'How markets work' covers section 3.1; Paper 2 'How the economy works' covers section 3.2. Each paper is 1 hour 30 minutes and 80 marks. There is no coursework or non-exam assessment — the entire qualification is examined, which makes every topic revisable. (Source: AQA specification 8136, section 2.2.)

Assessment objectives: AO1 (knowledge and understanding), AO2 (apply knowledge to a range of contexts), AO3 (analyse and evaluate economic evidence, make informed judgements). AO3 carries the extended-response and evaluation marks, so the 9- and 12-mark questions are where grades are won and lost. (Source: AQA specification 8136, section 4.2.)

Quantitative skills are worth a minimum of 15% of the overall marks (section 6 of the spec). Students must be able to calculate and interpret percentages, percentage change, price elasticity, index numbers (CPI), and read data from tables and charts. Build calculation practice into every relevant lesson, not just an isolated 'maths' lesson.

Both papers use data-response stimulus material (tables, charts, short extracts). Application marks (AO2) require students to USE the data and refer to the named context, not answer generically. Teach students to quote a figure or trend from the source in applied answers.

Diagrams are central to Economics. Demand and supply diagrams, production possibility diagrams, and the effect of shifts must be drawn accurately and labelled (axes, curves, equilibrium, the direction of any shift). Even where the written paper cannot show a diagram in revision content, the underlying logic (what shifts, which way, what happens to price and quantity) must be taught explicitly in prose.
current_spec_changes: AQA GCSE Economics (8136) is a linear qualification, first teaching 2017, first exams 2019, assessed in the summer series only. The examinable content (sections 3.1 and 3.2) is stable. (Source: AQA specification 8136, front matter and section 2.)

Economics uses live, changeable data — the Bank of England base rate, the CPI inflation rate, the UK unemployment rate, GDP growth and the inflation target. Content should teach the CURRENT framework (e.g. the 2% CPI inflation target set for the Bank of England; the Monetary Policy Committee setting Bank Rate) and use illustrative rather than dated specific figures, because the actual numbers move every year. Where a specific figure is used it must be checkable and clearly framed as an example at a point in time.

The European Union is named in the spec as the key example of a free-trade agreement (3.2.4.3). Post-Brexit the UK is no longer an EU member; teach the EU as the worked example of a free-trade bloc and the single market, and treat the UK's trading relationship neutrally and factually.
pedagogical_notes: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (+8 months) — explicitly model the chain-of-reasoning that Economics rewards: 'interest rates rise -> borrowing becomes more expensive and saving more attractive -> consumer spending and business investment fall -> aggregate demand falls -> inflationary pressure eases'. Students do not chain reasoning automatically; the 6/9/12-mark marks depend on it. (Source: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning Guidance Report.)

EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — Economics is dense with precise vocabulary that everyday English blurs: demand vs quantity demanded, production vs productivity, real vs nominal, fiscal vs monetary, deficit vs debt, income vs wealth. Teach a tight glossary at the top of each lesson and drill it with flashcards; imprecise synonyms lose marks. (Source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report.)

Worked examples for the quantitative skills — model each calculation type (percentage change, PED, PES, index numbers, reading a balance-of-payments table) step by step before students attempt a fresh one. Quantitative skills are 15% of marks and are highly trainable. (Source: EEF Metacognition guidance; quantitative-skills pedagogy.)

Dual coding for the core diagrams — demand and supply, shifts, equilibrium, the PPD, and the economic cycle are all visual. Pair every diagram concept with a worded cause-and-effect explanation and have students reproduce both the picture and the chain from memory. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit; Sweller cognitive load theory.)

Concrete, current real-world anchors — petrol prices and PED, the housing market and demand shifts, the minimum wage and the labour market, the Bank of England changing interest rates, a supermarket price war and competition. Tie every abstract model to a market a 15-16 year old recognises. (Source: EEF Cognitive Science Approaches in the Classroom report.)

Evaluation scaffolds — teach a repeatable evaluation toolkit for the 9- and 12-mark questions: it depends on the SIZE of the change, the TIME period (short vs long run), ELASTICITY, the STATE of the economy (boom vs recession), and WHO is affected (consumers, producers, government, workers). Students who carry this checklist into every evaluation reliably reach the top band. (Source: EEF guidance on chains of reasoning; A-level-to-GCSE evaluation pedagogy.)

gaps: There is no non-exam assessment in GCSE Economics — the qualification is two written papers, so every part of the specification is covered by this revision build with no project work excluded.

Specific live economic figures (the current Bank Rate, the latest CPI inflation rate, the UK unemployment rate, current GDP growth) are taught as framework + illustrative examples rather than fixed numbers, because they change every year. The fact-check pass verifies any specific figure used; teachers should refresh current data each year from the ONS and the Bank of England.
